en: The one now facing him,
Is I, Külchoro,
From the day Külchoro mounted a horse,
Sired by my father Almambet,
And borne by my hapless mother,
The fairy maiden Aruuke,
How many fearsome foes have I seen!
How many dire afflictions have I faced
From those who would slaughter every last
Descendant of Khan Manas!
No man dared confront me,
No enemy I faced defeated me.
Khans who rode against me died,
Many mighty warriors died.
Saying, “I will eagerly wage war,”
Khans of China fell.
Coming to grapple with me,
How many giants and ogres lay slain!
Orphaned of mother and father,
I wandered until I came of age.
Joining the people as best I could,
I matured and became a man,
Becoming the equal of heroic sons,
While our uncle was the sovereign khan,
And watchful foes were laid low,
I went on wrestling,
And no champion who came could defeat me.
Our fathers and forefathers,
Never surrendered their comrades’ lives.
From the day I became Külchoro,
From the day I mounted the steed Külüstan,
I wheeled my spear and broke the ranks,
My fortunes were set right by the unseen,
And anyone who fought me vanished.
When I stood glaring in fury,
No enemy dared confront me.
Of all the sons born to mankind,
None remained who dared oppose me.
Black within and blue without,
I did not meet my doom and die.
Never in all the world had I seen
Such an enemy as this infidel,
This son of a monster.
Brave Kyyaz, son of Bagysh,
He too is of Kyrgyz stock.
When he girded his waist firmly,
The two khans Chynkozho and Toltoi,
When they came to exact this blood-price,
Loosed arrows like falling rain,
Firing shots and starting strife,
When they came bringing calamity,
Our hearts burned and flames engulfed us,
They raised their banner on grassy ground,
And Kanchoro was our own kinsman.
That vicious swine began the quarrel,
Opening our flank and ruining everything,
Bringing disgrace and dividing the people,
Our people fled and scattered,
Our fortress was shattered.
Our hearts were trampled by evil,
And before the eyes of many enemies,
We now walk exposed like this.
When my noble uncle Semetey
Found the two of us,
He had ninety beasts slaughtered for a feast,
And gave us matching names,
Feeding us rump fat and horse mane,
Calling us inseparable brothers,
He had us equally suckled
At Kanykei’s breast,
And called sons of the noble one.
Yet Kanchoro, who had lived so,
Came out of the ravines,
Ravaging the land and slaughtering the people,
That swine rose as an enemy,
An abomination arose from our own hearth,
An enemy arose from our own kin,
Steeping poison for my destruction,
And thus brought about my downfall.
He told Kyyaz, son of Bagysh,
“Drive so-and-so here.”
God must have struck the fool.
Shamelessly exposing himself and ruining all,
He had become an enemy.
To the Zhediger of Zheti-Özön,
A peaceful people resting in their land,
With six fleet horses
And a letter no larger than a palm,
He sent word to wage war without delay,
So mountain-like Toltoi and Chynkozho
Would come and take revenge,
So the honorable would witness it,
So brave Kyyaz would cease to be a man
And die rather than remain alive.
Yesterday, when the Zhediger overran us,
And the people were devastated,
Saying, “My own younger brother became my foe,”
The magnanimous lion took offense.
When my elder brother was beguiled
By Kökmonchok, daughter of a peri,
And vanished into the unseen,
I was entangled in a net of ropes
And fell into the enemy’s hands.
Truly ensnared, I braced myself,
But fell into Kanchoro’s hands.
My own kinsman became my enemy,
And grief filled my heart.
My heart boiled like fire,
Deprived of my protector,
And there my cherished hopes froze.
May no believer die
As I suffered humiliation;
If my God creates a living soul,
May He spare His servant such torment.
They scorched my breast over fire,
And sliced my hide like leather.
They ignored my pleas and words,
And robbed me thus of all my strength.
They dug a pit as my prison,
And stripped off my robe as plunder.
They had my hands bound behind my back,
While my eyes blazed like a lion’s.
My own brother Kanchoro
Thus made my misery boil.
He had holes pierced through my elbows,
As though I had killed
His father, Khan Chubak.
He gave me to ninety fearsome champions
To crush and pulp my breast,
Imprisoned me in the raging waters,
And gave me to ninety fearsome champions
To club and beat me.
Though we were kin raised together,
He burned me with smokeless fire,
Tormenting me,
And would not hear me when I pleaded,
Leaving my eyes imploring,
Swelling my flesh grotesquely,
Thus making my misery boil.
Not from a stranger or an outsider,
But from my own kin I suffered this wonder.
“Kill him if he so much as stirs,”
He ordered guards stationed beside me.
My right shoulder and my left,
Where my two arms drew their strength,
He had gouged through from behind.
My two eyes blazed,
So did my misery boil.
When I suffered such torment,
Had sorrow weighed upon my bones?
Having faced fresh calamity here,
Had my courage deserted me?
Had my joints weakened and strength departed,
Had the smiting God struck me?
They gouged my shoulder and placed a writ there,
Saying, “Let him be the slave of slaves,”
And named me Denekul.
My two hands were bound,
My two eyes were blazing,
My tiny life cried out,
Every bone in me cracked.
When my lion’s head burned,
For nine years under Kyyaz
I lived as a woodcutter.
A deep pit seems to have been dug;
Our misery truly came to the boil.
My days passed in slavery
While I served brave Kyyaz.
Whatever I bit became a bullet,
Whatever I grasped became an ember.
I regarded a lamb’s fat as frozen treasure,
Carrying firewood for nine years,
And found hell terribly vast.
Only a spoonful of blood remained in me,
My flesh was but a blue, raw scrap.
Carrying firewood on my back,
My collarbones were rubbed raw.
In this living hell,
My heart ached so.
My heart chilled into ice,
My tiny life throbbed with pain.
Torn apart by anxious thoughts,
The tears flowing from both eyes
Spilled down my chest.
Facing hell itself,
Carrying firewood for nine years,
My lion spirit was reduced to this,
Enslaved for so many years,
Until each passing day sank into night,
I bore firewood upon my back.
Whenever Kyyaz came out shouting,
At the memory of it I would faint away.
The earth was too hard to enter,
Yet life was too sweet to die.
Pierced and divided by sorrow,
My tears poured down,
Sixty hells and a thousand afflictions
Appeared close above my head.
While my heroic uncle lived,
He towered over all the people.
Yet in the hands of brave Kyyaz,
I suffered disgrace for many years.
The vile, cunning enemy exhausted me,
And my days passed in slavery.
I withered under suffering,
Wasted pale with yellow sickness.
My collarbones were rubbed raw,
And the flesh of my sides was torn.
It became clear that this darkened,
Treacherous world had left me behind.
There is no forest for the blind,
Alive today and gone tomorrow,
And I had no strength left to gird my waist.
When I escaped my suffering,
My valiant uncle was no longer there.
When I lamented, my tongue poured forth,
While my two eyes blazed.
I could do nothing by my own will,
For my two hands were bound.
Brave Kyyaz’s herd of horses,
His surging, gleaming herd!
It thundered down from above,
And tending horses was hell.
For the herdsman himself,
I hurriedly carried firewood.
Unable to face the day of death,
As the day grew late and the sun set,
That herdsman clubbed me
Until my skin was tanned raw.
When dawn broke bright,
I danced like a Kalmyk.
When the sun reached midmorning,
I slung a milk pail around my neck.
The hell of this world—
This is how I endured it.
I carried birch firewood,
While the herdsman drank his fill within.
He made me gnaw clean and swallow
The knucklebones of two horses.
I was imprisoned by a hostile slave,
And beaten by the herdsman.
Saying, “The slave has grown insolent,”
They plundered what little I possessed.
The garden-city of our fortune was bound,
And our destiny was broken then.
Disgraced, my eyes still blazed;
Thus did my misery boil.
I suffered torment from the enemy,
And cruel humiliation crushed my soul.
Only a spoonful of blood remained in me,
My flesh was but a blue, raw scrap.
At that time I thought,
“The death of this wretched head
Has arrived without my dying.”
I thought, “The strength and vigor
Of my steel-boned body are gone.”
